content: The outer ear is the external part of the auditory system, comprising the pinna, concha, and auditory meatus. Its primary function is to collect sound energy from the environment and direct it toward the eardrum, also known as the tympanic membrane. This specific amplification makes humans particularly sensitive to sounds in this frequency range. However, it also increases their susceptibility to acoustic injuries and hearing loss at these frequencies. Notably, most human speech sounds fall within the bandwidth around 3 kHz, which aligns with this sensitivity. The pinna, also referred to as the auricle, is the visible external part of the ear. Its role is to gather and focus sound waves. In many mammals, the pinna can be moved using auricular muscles to direct hearing toward specific sources, similar to how they can adjust their gaze. However, most humans lack the ability to move their pinna in this way, unlike many other mammals. Sound waves collected by the pinna travel into the ear canal, also known as the external auditory meatus. This canal is a simple tubular structure that leads to the middle ear. It further amplifies sound frequencies, particularly those in the range of 3 kHz to 12 kHz.
